title: Hardware and disk space management
lead: DBMS layers, storage hierarchy, page I/O and the disk space manager.

sections.title: DBMS architecture
sections.html:
The query-planning layer parses and checks SQL, then chooses an executable plan. Operator execution runs the plan over records. File and index management organises those records into pages and access structures.

Buffer management moves pages between persistent storage and memory. Disk space management maps logical page requests to physical storage operations. Each layer exposes an interface and hides the representation below it.

Concurrency control and recovery cross these layers. They coordinate simultaneous operations and restore a valid database after failures. Their correctness depends on how memory changes, page writes and log writes are ordered.

PDF pp. 1–10

sections.title: Storage hierarchy and magnetic disks
sections.html:
Disk-oriented DBMSs keep the database on non-volatile storage and process data in volatile memory. Registers, caches and DRAM offer low latency but limited capacity; SSDs and HDDs provide larger persistent storage. A page read or write transfers a block of bytes, rather than an individual field.

For an HDD, access time has three components: seek time, rotational delay and transfer time. The slide’s 8 KB example sums 3.40 ms, 2.00 ms and approximately 0.05 ms to obtain 5.45 ms. These are parameters of that device example.

Random reads repeatedly pay seek and rotational overhead. Sequential reads amortise that overhead across neighbouring blocks. Physical placement and prefetching therefore affect scan performance.

PDF pp. 11–19

sections.title: SSDs and page-oriented storage
sections.html:
An SSD removes mechanical seek and rotation, but reads, writes and erasures still have different granularities and costs. NAND flash is erased in blocks larger than the read/write page. Small updates can cause write amplification; wear levelling distributes erase activity.

Device bandwidth, endurance and price figures in the slides describe the cited hardware context. The design conclusion is that locality and I/O volume matter on both SSDs and HDDs, even though their penalties differ.

A database file consists of pages containing records. The DBMS seeks spatial control over placement and temporal control over transfers. Reducing the number of I/Os and using more useful data per I/O are central goals.

PDF pp. 20–25

sections.title: Disk space manager
sections.html:
The disk space manager allocates and deallocates pages, reads pages into memory and writes pages back. Each page has a logical page ID. The layer maintains the mapping from that identifier to a physical file and byte offset.

Higher layers can request a sequence of pages. The manager aims to make consecutive logical pages efficient to scan by arranging their physical locations appropriately. A logical database file may span several operating-system files or devices.

This interface hides filesystem and device details from buffer management. “Next page” expresses an intended locality property; actual performance still depends on allocation and the storage system.

PDF pp. 26–29

quiz.question: Under the exercise’s model, how long does reading 200 contiguous pages take?
quiz.explanation: Seek time plus rotational latency is 7 ms. Transferring 200 pages takes 20 ms, giving a total of 27 ms under the stated assumptions.
